lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: The bandit Sostratus here — throw him into Pyriphlegethon. The temple-robber — let the Chimera tear him apart. The tyrant, Hermes — stretch him out next to Tityus and let the vultures have his liver as well. And the rest of you — the good ones — off to the Elysian Fields at once. Go take up residence in the Islands of the Blessed. You've earned it.
lines.note: Brisk, docket-clearing energy. Minos is in full sentencing mode — no preamble, just rulings.

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Hear me out, Minos. Tell me if what I'm about to say seems just.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Hear you out. Now. After the verdict. Sostratus, you were examined. You were found to be a thoroughly bad man who killed a great number of people. This is settled.

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Granted. But consider whether the punishment is actually just.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Entirely just, if paying what one owes is just.

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Then answer me one thing, Minos. One short thing.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Short, yes. We have others to get through.
lines.note: Slightly impatient, but he grants it — Minos is fair.

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Everything I did in life — did I do it by choice, or had the Fates already spun it out for me?

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: So all of us — the ones you call virtuous, and the ones you call wicked — we were all of us just carrying out her orders?

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Yes. Clotho assigned each person their actions at birth.

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Right. So. If a man is compelled by someone else to commit a killing — someone he cannot refuse, someone who is forcing him — an executioner, say, or a soldier: one obeying a judge, the other obeying a tyrant. Who do you hold responsible for the death?
lines.note: Sostratus has dropped the act entirely. He's arguing like a philosopher and he knows it.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Clearly the judge, or the tyrant. You wouldn't blame the sword itself — it's just an instrument, a tool in the hands of whoever provided the original cause.
lines.note: Minos answers without thinking — and then, just slightly, feels the trap closing.

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Good. I appreciate the generosity of the example. [pause] Now: if a master sends a servant to deliver gold or silver, who gets the credit? Who do you list as the benefactor?
lines.note: Sostratus lets the silence do the work.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: The one who sent him, Sostratus. The carrier was just the delivery man.
lines.note: Minos sees exactly where this is going.

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Then do you see the injustice? You punish us — the instruments, the servants doing whatever Clotho commanded — and you reward those others who were equally just carrying out somebody else's goodness. Because nobody can argue with orders given under absolute necessity. That much surely cannot be disputed.
lines.note: Calm, almost gentle. The most dangerous kind of argument.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: [long pause] Sostratus. If you looked closely enough, you'd find a great many things in the universe that don't quite hold up to scrutiny. [pause] Nevertheless. You've earned something for the question — because it turns out you're not just a bandit, you're also something of a philosopher. Hermes — release him. No further punishment. [beat] And make sure he doesn't spend the rest of eternity teaching the other corpses to ask the same thing.
lines.note: Dry, resigned, genuinely amused. The admission is real but limited — Minos doesn't overturn the system, he just lets one man out. The final warning is the line that gets the laugh.
